title: Baba Ram Singh and the Namdharis
hook: a movement in white clothes, reciting the Name and boycotting British goods

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nirankari, and your line was back to the formless. Which extra step did you take out of a habit? Today, a second reformer, with a firmer edge. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

White cloth. That's what you'd notice first. A crowd gathers in a village in the Punjab, and everyone is dressed in plain white, with turbans tied straight across the forehead. They're reciting the Name together. Some of them, caught up in it, cry out loud, and the neighbors start calling them Kukas, from those cries. Their leader asks them to do something bold for the time: don't use the British post, don't go to British courts, don't wear foreign cloth. The leader is Baba Ram Singh. Today: Namdhari.
screen: `A CROWD DRESSED IN WHITE.` → `RECITING THE NAME ALOUD.` → `NO BRITISH POST, COURTS OR CLOTH.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Namdhari is the name the movement chose for itself, and its followers understand it as one who holds the Name. Kuka was the neighbors' nickname, tied, the story goes, to the cries that rose up during their recitation. Second, the teacher. Baba Ram Singh came from the village of Bhaini, in the Ludhiana district, and he had served as a soldier before he turned to teaching. He called people to the Name, to the Khalsa's discipline, and to plain living: white clothes, no meat, no alcohol, honest work. He spoke against the dowry and against killing baby daughters, and he held simple weddings, sometimes for many couples at once, without heavy cost. Third, the refusal. Under British rule, Baba Ram Singh told his followers to stay away from British schools, courts, post and goods. Settle your disputes among yourselves. Weave your own cloth. Some historians see in this an early form of the boycotts of India's later freedom movement. The British watched him closely. Fourth, a fair word on difference. Namdharis hold that the line of living Gurus continued after Guru Gobind Singh, through Baba Balak Singh and Baba Ram Singh. The Akal Takht and the wider Khalsa Panth hold that Guru Gobind Singh passed the Guruship to the Guru Granth Sahib, and that no person holds it after him. This lesson tells his story, and leaves that question to each community. A simple rule, kept firmly, can say more than a long argument.
screen: `NAMDHARI — ONE WHO HOLDS THE NAME.` · `WHITE CLOTHES AND PLAIN LIVING.` · `NO BRITISH COURTS, POST OR CLOTH.` · `WHO HOLDS THE GURUSHIP.` · then, large: `SIMPLE AND FIRM.`

segments.voice: Two minutes in something plain. If you can, notice what you're wearing right now. Not to judge it. Just notice: the color, the weight, whether it's simple or busy. Then let your attention move from the cloth to the breath underneath it. Slow and even. Ask yourself one quiet question: what's one plain, firm thing I could keep, without explaining it to anyone? Let the answer come or not. If you pray, you can repeat Waheguru on each breath, as the Namdharis recite the Name. The bell holds the time.
Namdhari. One who holds the Name; the followers of Baba Ram Singh, dressed in white, also nicknamed Kukas. Today's word.
Your line: simple and firm. Today, wear something simple, and keep one small promise to yourself without bending it. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Namdhari Sikhs wear white, tie their turbans straight across the forehead, recite the Name together, and remember Baba Ram Singh as a teacher of plain living and of refusing British goods and courts.

fork.setup: you follow Baba Ram Singh, and a neighbor wrongs you. where do you take the dispute?
options: to the British court in town.
to your own community to settle.

original.note: Namdhari, one who holds the Name.

trapdoor: what you thought: Namdharis are Sikhs who wear white.
what it means: one who holds the Name; Baba Ram Singh's followers, known for plain living and recitation of the Name.
what a scholar hears: an early refusal of British courts, post and goods, and a community that holds the line of living Gurus continued, which the Akal Takht does not.

sources.work: Harbans Singh (ed.), The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism

notes: Please check the fairness of the paragraph on the Guruship: Namdhari belief in a continuing line of living Gurus (Balak Singh, Ram Singh) versus the mainstream Sikh position (Guru Granth Sahib as Guru). Namdhari readers should recognize themselves.
Baba Ram Singh's earlier army service, Bhaini (now Bhaini Sahib, Ludhiana), and his stance on dowry, female infanticide and mass simple weddings: confirm.
Etymology nam + dhari and kook as the source of 'Kuka': confirm.
'Historians later pointed to this as an early form of the boycotts': a historiographic claim; confirm or soften.
